body:
India under East India Company rule

By the middle of the 19th century, the English East India Company had become the dominant political and military power in India. It directly administered large territories and exercised considerable influence over many Indian princely states. Its expansion had weakened traditional rulers, changed landownership and revenue arrangements, and created dissatisfaction among several sections of Indian society.

In 1857, a major armed uprising challenged this authority. It began with the rebellion of Indian soldiers serving in the Company's army and developed into a wider movement involving rulers, landlords, peasants, religious leaders and sections of the urban population.

Sepoy mutiny and popular rebellion

A sepoy was an Indian soldier serving in the Company's army. A mutiny occurs when soldiers collectively disobey or turn against their military authorities. The events of 1857 began with military mutinies, but in important regions they developed into a popular rebellion as civilians also challenged Company rule.

Why the uprising had several causes

The uprising cannot be explained by a single incident. The Company had annexed kingdoms, weakened ruling families and disturbed existing political arrangements. Peasants and landholders resented revenue demands and the loss of land. Soldiers complained about service conditions and interference with religious practices. Many people also feared that colonial policies threatened their religious and social customs.

These grievances were connected. A soldier recruited from a village could be dissatisfied with his military service while his family suffered from high land revenue or the annexation of its home region. Consequently, discontent within the army could reinforce dissatisfaction outside it.

Why different names are used

The uprising is commonly called the Revolt of 1857, the Uprising of 1857, the Sepoy Mutiny or the First War of Independence. These names emphasise different aspects of the same historical events.

The expression Sepoy Mutiny draws attention to its military beginnings. However, it is too narrow to describe places such as Awadh, where peasants, landlords and townspeople also participated extensively. First War of Independence expresses the importance of resistance to foreign rule, although anti-British uprisings had occurred before 1857 and the rebels did not share a single modern national programme.

Geographical extent

The strongest centres were in northern and central India, especially Delhi, Meerut, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi and parts of Bihar. Resistance also appeared in Gujarat and other regions, but its scale and character varied considerably. Large parts of the subcontinent did not experience a comparable sustained uprising.

The revolt failed to remove British authority, but it brought an end to the Company's administration of India. In 1858, governing authority was transferred to the British Crown.

Prelims focus

  • The major uprising began in 1857 under East India Company rule.
  • Its military beginnings developed into wider civilian resistance in several regions.
  • Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi and Bihar were important centres.
  • Company administration ended in 1858, although British colonial rule continued.
  • Trap: The uprising was neither confined to soldiers everywhere nor uniformly spread across India.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 5, 'When People Rebel: 1857 and After', printed pp. 51–61, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Rebels and the Raj', section 'Pattern of the Rebellion'; GCERT, History, Std 12, 'Revolt of 1857', printed pp. 24–33.]

title: The Uprising of 1857: Nature, Background and Historical Importance

body:
How Company expansion created political resentment

The East India Company expanded its control through wars, treaties, political intervention and annexation. Indian rulers who lost their territories also lost revenue, authority and status. Their courts, soldiers, dependants and officials could lose their livelihoods. Thus, the effects of annexation extended beyond individual royal families.

Two major British policies must be distinguished: the Doctrine of Lapse and annexation on the grounds of alleged misgovernment. They were not the same policy.

The Doctrine of Lapse

Under Governor-General Lord Dalhousie, the Company used the Doctrine of Lapse to annex certain dependent princely states when their rulers died without a natural male heir. In these cases, the Company refused to recognise an adopted successor for the purpose of inheriting sovereignty.

Important examples include Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur. The policy caused resentment because adoption was an accepted practice in many Indian ruling families.

Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi wanted the Company to recognise her adopted son as heir to the kingdom after her husband's death. The Company's refusal became a major political grievance associated with Jhansi.

Awadh was annexed for a different stated reason

Awadh was annexed in 1856. The Company justified the annexation by alleging misgovernment under Nawab Wajid Ali Shah. Awadh was not annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.

The annexation removed the Nawab, disturbed the position of many local landholders and affected soldiers whose families belonged to the region. Consequently, Awadh became one of the most important centres of civilian participation during the rebellion.

Other important political grievances

Person or stateBritish actionCause of resentment
JhansiDoctrine of LapseRefusal to recognise an adopted heir to the throne
AwadhAnnexation in 1856 on grounds of misgovernmentRemoval of the Nawab and disruption of political and landed interests
Nana SahebRefusal to continue the pension of his adoptive father, Peshwa Baji Rao IILoss of an expected pension and political status
Mughal dynastyProgressive reduction of imperial authority and statusThreat to the dynasty's remaining position

Nana Saheb's grievance concerned the continuation of his adoptive father's pension. It should not be confused with the Doctrine of Lapse, which concerned succession to certain princely states.

The Mughal emperor's declining position

Although the Mughal emperor no longer exercised extensive territorial power, the dynasty retained historical prestige. The Company removed the emperor's name from its coins and planned to end recognition of the Mughal royal title after Bahadur Shah Zafar.

When rebel soldiers reached Delhi in May 1857, they turned to Bahadur Shah Zafar because his position could provide a familiar symbol of political authority. His acceptance helped give the rebellion a wider political significance.

Prelims focus

  • Lord Dalhousie is associated with the Doctrine of Lapse.
  • Jhansi, Satara and Nagpur were annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.
  • Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the stated ground of misgovernment.
  • Nana Saheb was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II and sought continuation of his pension.
  • Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal emperor.
  • Trap: Awadh's annexation and Nana Saheb's pension dispute were not applications of the Doctrine of Lapse.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, 'From Trade to Territory', and Chapter 5, 'When People Rebel', printed pp. 51–52; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Rebels and the Raj', section 'Awadh in Revolt'; GCERT, History, Std 12, 'Revolt of 1857', section on political causes, printed pp. 24–26.]

title: Political Causes: Annexation, Princely States and the Loss of Authority

body:
Land revenue and the distress of cultivators

Company rule changed how land revenue was assessed and collected in many regions. Cultivators faced high demands, and collection could be rigid even when crops failed or agricultural income declined. Some peasants borrowed money to pay revenue or meet household needs. Failure to repay debts could result in the loss of land.

These grievances mattered during 1857 because a rebellion against the Company could also become a struggle against unpopular local arrangements. Some rebels attacked revenue offices and records associated with taxes, debts and property claims.

Why landholders and taluqdars joined

A taluqdar was a substantial landholder who held rights and exercised influence over a local territory. In Awadh, British annexation and subsequent revenue arrangements weakened or displaced many taluqdars. This encouraged some of them to support the rebels.

Their interests were not identical to those of poor cultivators. A taluqdar might seek restoration of authority and land rights, while a peasant might seek relief from revenue burdens or creditors. Nevertheless, both could oppose the Company's administration.

Economic difficulties among artisans and traders

Traditional manufacturing and craft occupations also experienced difficulties under colonial economic arrangements. Competition from British manufactured goods and changes in trade weakened several established livelihoods. This contributed to wider dissatisfaction, although its effects varied among industries and regions.

Economic distress was therefore a long-term contributing cause, not a single event that immediately started the uprising.

Administrative grievances

Many Indians criticised the conduct of Company officials, unequal treatment, limited access to higher positions, and the cost or unfamiliarity of courts and administrative procedures. These concerns added to dissatisfaction with foreign rule.

Social reform and fears of religious interference

The British introduced or supported changes in social practices, promoted English education and permitted Christian missionary activity. Measures associated with the abolition of sati and the legal recognition of widow remarriage formed part of this changing environment.

Reactions to these changes differed. Some Indians supported reform, while others feared that the government intended to undermine established religious and social customs. These fears became especially powerful when combined with rumours circulating among soldiers and civilians.

Under a law enacted in 1850, a person's change of religion did not automatically deprive that person of inheritance rights. Although the measure protected property rights, it increased fears among some groups that the government was encouraging conversion to Christianity.

Distinguish an action from a fear

The existence of missionary activity or a law protecting converts' inheritance rights is a historical fact. The belief that the British intended to convert all Indians was a fear held by some people. An examination statement should not present that fear as a proven universal government policy.

The link between civilians and soldiers

Many Company sepoys came from agricultural families, particularly in regions such as Awadh. They could experience military grievances while also hearing about revenue difficulties and political changes at home. Thus, discontent in the countryside helped reinforce the anger of soldiers.

Prelims focus

  • High land revenue, indebtedness and loss of land contributed to rural dissatisfaction.
  • Awadh's taluqdars were affected by annexation and changes in landed rights.
  • Competition from British manufactured goods affected traditional crafts and industries.
  • The 1850 inheritance law protected inheritance rights despite religious conversion.
  • Fear of interference with religious customs contributed to the uprising.
  • Trap: Not every Indian opposed social reform, and rumours about conversion must be distinguished from established policies.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 5, 'When People Rebel', printed pp. 51–54; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Rebels and the Raj', sections 'Awadh in Revolt' and 'What the Rebels Wanted'; GCERT, History, Std 12, 'Revolt of 1857', sections on economic, administrative and social-religious causes, printed pp. 24–26.]

title: Economic, Administrative, Social and Religious Causes of the Uprising

body:
Why Indian sepoys became dissatisfied

Indian soldiers formed a large part of the East India Company's armies. They fought in Company campaigns and helped maintain its territorial authority. Yet many sepoys believed that they were treated less favourably than European soldiers.

Important military grievances included lower pay and allowances, restricted opportunities for promotion, disrespectful treatment by some British officers and rules that conflicted with religious practices.

In some circumstances, sepoys also resented changes in allowances associated with military service. These complaints accumulated over time and weakened confidence in their employers.

The question of overseas service

Some Indian soldiers believed that crossing the sea could compromise their caste or religious standing. This made compulsory overseas service a sensitive issue.

The General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 required new recruits to accept service overseas if ordered. It was particularly controversial in the Bengal Army, from which many of the later rebels came.

Which soldiers did the 1856 requirement concern?

The new overseas-service condition applied to new recruits. It should not be described as a rule that automatically and retrospectively imposed the same requirement on every existing sepoy.

The Enfield rifle and its cartridges

The immediate controversy centred on cartridges used with the new Enfield rifle. Soldiers were expected to bite open the paper cartridge before loading the weapon. A rumour spread that the cartridges had been greased with cow and pig fat.

This was deeply objectionable to many soldiers. Cows had religious importance for Hindus, while pigs were regarded as unclean by Muslims. The suspicion that sepoys would have to put the alleged grease in their mouths intensified fears that their religious practices were being deliberately violated.

The controversy mattered not simply because a new rifle had been introduced, but because distrust of Company intentions was already widespread. An explanation that attributes the entire uprising to the cartridges alone overlooks its political, economic and military background.

Long-term causes and the immediate trigger

Historians distinguish the underlying causes from the immediate trigger. Underlying causes made people increasingly dissatisfied over several years. The cartridge issue caused a direct confrontation between soldiers and military authorities in 1857.

Why the controversy crossed religious boundaries

The alleged use of cow and pig fat offended different religious sensitivities at the same time. Because Hindu and Muslim sepoys served in the same armies, the rumour provided a shared grievance even where other political and social interests differed.

The precise composition of particular cartridges should not be treated as an undisputed fact merely because the rumour spread widely. For understanding the uprising, the historically established point is that soldiers suspected the use of objectionable animal fat and reacted strongly to that belief.

Prelims focus

  • The controversial weapon was the Enfield rifle.
  • Sepoys suspected its cartridges of being greased with cow and pig fat.
  • The cartridges were associated with a drill requiring soldiers to bite them open.
  • The General Service Enlistment Act, 1856 concerned acceptance of overseas service by new recruits.
  • Military grievances included pay, allowances, promotion and religious concerns.
  • Trap: The cartridge issue was an immediate trigger, not the sole cause of the uprising.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 5, 'When People Rebel', printed pp. 52–56; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Rebels and the Raj', section 'Rumours and Prophecies'; GCERT, History, Std 12, 'Revolt of 1857', sections on military causes and the immediate cause, printed pp. 26–28.]
